deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page solves the trinomial F t^f = G t^g + H t^h with Gauss's addition/subtraction logarithm tables. This page studies the same trinomial in the form Fx^f + Gx^g + Hx^h = 0 with f > g > h. It covers three things: (i) when there is a double root, (ii) which leading terms give the roots, with the rate of convergence of the resulting series, and (iii) the polar form of the complex roots. The next page (283) works the example x^7 - 3x^2 + 2 = 0 numerically.

(1) Double-root condition. The filling-in here is mine. Put A = Fx^f, B = Gx^g, C = Hx^h. A double root satisfies A + B + C = 0 and x p'(x) = fA + gB + hC = 0. Hence A : B : C = (g-h) : (h-f) : (f-g), i.e. Fx^f = λ(g-h), Gx^g = λ(h-f), Hx^h = λ(f-g). Raise these to the powers g-h, h-f, f-g and multiply. The exponents of λ add to 0. The exponents of x add to f(g-h) + g(h-f) + h(f-g) = 0. This gives T := (F/(g-h))^(g-h) (G/(h-f))^(h-f) (H/(f-g))^(f-g) = 1.

Gauss writes P = (-F/(g-h))^(g-h) (G/(h-f))^(h-f) (H/(f-g))^(f-g) = 1. He marks in the margin that the sign of the first factor is deliberate ('so, rücksichtlich der Zeichen, absichtlich'). Thus P = (-1)^(g-h) T. For the example f=7, g=2, h=0 he gets P = (1/4)(7/3)^7 (2/5)^5 = 6588344/6834375 ≈ 0.964, as on the next page.

(2) Regimes, with f-g > 0 and g-h > 0.
- If P < 1: the f-g large roots are approximated by (-G/F)^(1/(f-g)) (balancing the F and G terms). The g-h small roots are approximated by (-H/G)^(1/(g-h)) (balancing the G and H terms).
- If P > 1: the middle term is negligible, and all f-h roots come approximately ('genäh.') from (-H/F)^(1/(f-h)).
- Convergence of the correcting series. My check: scale x = x0·y and note that P is homogeneous in the perturbing coefficient. In case 1 the successive terms then fall in the ratio 1 : P^(1/(f-g)) and 1 : P^(1/(g-h)), as Gauss states. In case 2 the ratio is P^(1/(f-h)) : 1 (see errors).

(3) Complex roots x = r(cos θ + i sin θ), real coefficients. Put a = Fr^f, b = Gr^g, c = Hr^h. Multiply a e^{ifθ} + b e^{igθ} + c e^{ihθ} = 0 by e^{-ihθ}, e^{-igθ}, e^{-ifθ} in turn and take imaginary parts. This gives:
- a sin(f-h)θ + b sin(g-h)θ = 0,
- a sin(f-g)θ - c sin(g-h)θ = 0,
- b sin(f-g)θ + c sin(f-h)θ = 0.
Together these are Gauss's last line: r^f F / sin(g-h)θ = - r^g G / sin(f-h)θ = r^h H / sin(f-g)θ.

Taking quotients gives his three formulas:
- r^(f-g) = -(G/F) sin(g-h)θ / sin(f-h)θ,
- r^(g-h) = -(H/G) sin(f-h)θ / sin(f-g)θ,
- r^(f-h) = (H/F) sin(g-h)θ / sin(f-g)θ.
The third is the product of the first two.

Eliminating r between the first two (raise to powers g-h and f-g) gives the equation for θ alone: (-1)^(f-h) F^(g-h) H^(f-g) / G^(f-h) · sin^(f-h)((f-h)θ) / [sin^(f-g)((f-g)θ) sin^(g-h)((g-h)θ)] = 1. Here (-1)^(f-2g+h) = (-1)^(f-h). In the limit θ → 0 this reduces to the real double-root condition. Next page: for the example this is (32/2187) sin^7 7θ / (sin^5 5θ sin^2 2θ) = 1, solved as θ = 73°45'51.766'' with log r = 0.1207403, matching the root 0.3692 ± 1.2677 i.
errors: Sign convention: with the minus sign on F, P differs from the algebraically exact double-root expression T by (-1)^(g-h). 'P = 1' is exactly the double-root condition only when g-h is even, as in the worked example where g-h = 2, or under the sign convention Gauss explicitly flags as intentional. Only |P| matters for convergence.

Possible slip in the P > 1 convergence statement. Scaling x = (-H/F)^(1/(f-h))·y shows the series in the perturbing parameter converges like P^(1/(f-h)) : 1. The page appears to read P^(1/(g-h)) : 1, which is unless the series is arranged differently. The faint exponent should be checked on the original.
The 'a' between the factors of P, and the 'a' before F in the θ-equation, are struck out; they are not part of the formulas.
The θ- and r-formulas themselves check out correctly, including the sign (-1)^(f-h) obtained from (-1)^(f-2g+h) for integer exponents.

results.what: Double-root (discriminant-type) condition for the trinomial Fx^f+Gx^g+Hx^h: (F/(g-h))^(g-h)(G/(h-f))^(h-f)(H/(f-g))^(f-g)=1
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler/Lagrange era); explicit trinomial discriminant formulas are standard in 19th-century algebra

results.what: Criterion P<1 / P>1 deciding which pairs of terms dominate, with geometric convergence rates of the root-expansion series
results.modern_name: Newton-polygon / dominant-balance asymptotics; convergence of Lambert-Lagrange trinomial series
results.usually_credited_to: Lambert (1758), Lagrange (1770) for the series; convergence radii studied later (e.g. Eisenstein; 20th-century work on trinomials, Mellin)

results.what: Polar solution of complex roots of a real trinomial: θ from (-1)^(f-h)F^(g-h)H^(f-g)G^(h-f) sin^(f-h)(f-h)θ/(sin^(f-g)(f-g)θ sin^(g-h)(g-h)θ)=1, then r from the sine ratios
results.modern_name: Polar/trigonometric method for complex roots of trinomial equations
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss's own trinomial work (Göttingische gelehrte Anzeigen 1840s, using Gaussian logarithms) is generally cited; similar formulas appear in later 19th-century literature

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in, and published method for, solving trinomial equations with his logarithm tables (including complex roots) is known. This page is a careful working note: double-root criterion, convergence regimes, and polar equations for complex roots. It is a notable but expected unpublished detail, not a new result.

illustrative: for p=x^5-5x+t (f=5,g=1,h=0, F=1,G=-5,H=t) the discriminant vanishes exactly when T=(F/(g-h))^(g-h)(G/(h-f))^(h-f)(H/(f-g))^(f-g)=1, i.e. t^4 = 4^4 (t = ±4, with double roots at x = ±1)
θ ≈ 1.28743 rad (=73°45'51.77'') solves the θ-equation for x^7-3x^2+2
r^(f-g) = -(G/F) sin(g-h)θ/sin(f-h)θ gives r≈1.3204 and x≈0.3692+1.2677i is a root (residual ≈ 0)

transcription_corrections: Margin note reads 'so, rücksichtlich der Zeichen, absichtlich' (i.e. 'thus, regarding the signs, intentionally'), referring to the minus sign in -F/(g-h).
The '[-·-]' between the second and third factor of P is a struck-out 'a'; the trailing struck '=P' is a cancelled restatement.
In the θ-equation the 'a' before F^(g-h) is struck out.
Exponents in the sines should be read as powers of the sines: sin^(f-h)((f-h)θ), sin^(f-g)((f-g)θ), sin^(g-h)((g-h)θ).
'genäh.' (= genähert, approximately) is written above the P>1 line.
Struck word before 'P^(1/(g-h)) : 1' in the last line of the first section is a cancelled 'Reih...'.
The exponent in 'P^(1/(g-h)) : 1' (P>1 case) is faint; the mathematically expected exponent is 1/(f-h), so the original should be checked.
